chapter_theme: Natrinai 161 to 180: men going home and men about to leave, the friend's refusals of bards, dancers and night visits, and the jealousies of the married house.

161.reading: Going home with the king's hard work finished, the man tells his charioteer of the long straight road through the forest, where blue lilies open like eyes in every hill pool and the vengai sheds its flowers, and wonders whether the omen birds have already told of his coming to her, the honey-voiced woman who soothes their son with a pretence by pointing out strangers to him.
161.nuance: The hooves cut kaanthal petals that look like bangles (வளை என), and the next words wish her shoulders firm again (தோள் வலி யாப்ப): the road home is already undoing the slack bangles of her waiting. Pointing out strangers to the boy is read here as her passing them off as his father; the phrase is compressed.

colophon.thurai: வினை முற்றிப் பெயரும்தலைவன் தேர்ப்பாகன் கேட்ப சொல்லியது

thinai_evidence.note: a man returning over forest land to a wife who waits is mullai's waiting

comparisons.tenor: the blue lilies in the hill pools

162.reading: To the girl who weeps that she cannot bear to be alone at the painful evening when even the red-legged dove of the house joins its mate, and says she will come with him, the man answers that she, so delicate beside her mother in her famous father's great house, could hardly be strong enough for the waste where in summer the long hanging roots of the fig swing like a rope cradle in the west wind and stroke a sleeping she-elephant.
162.nuance: The refusal is tender: the one gentle thing he finds in the waste, a hanging root rocking a sleeping elephant like a cradle, recalls the nursed childhood he names in line 8. The doves of lines 1 and 2 come close to iraicchi (a pair joined at dusk), but the girl draws the sense herself (தனியே இருத்தல் ஆற்றேன்), so they stay scene.

colophon.thurai: உடன் போதுவல் என்ற தலைவிக்குத் தலைவன் சொற்றது

thinai_evidence.note: the girl asks to go with him across the waste

comparisons.tenor: the fig's long hanging roots swinging in the wind

163.reading: Glad that the marriage is settled, she says: may they breathe again at last, the pitiable blue-dark punnai and the lone bright kaithai of the shore grove, which suffered long, as her own heart did, while day and night, in the sand-laden wind, the shore lord's horses, bells ringing, climbed the moonlit dunes, horses that appear with the beauty of the sun rising at dawn.
163.nuance: The pity goes to the trees: the punnai and kaithai trampled by his night visits carry the cost of the secret love, and the marriage frees them as it frees her heart (என் நெஞ்சம் போல). Whether அளிய (the pitiable ones) is the trees or the horses is not fixed.

colophon.thurai: வரைவு மலிந்து சொல்லியது

thinai_evidence.note: the shore grove of punnai and kaithai

comparisons.tenor: the punnai and kaithai trampled night after night

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon names no speaker; the first person (என் நெஞ்சம்) points to the girl

164.reading: The friend reminds the girl that when he left in the season the rain had deserted and the sun cracked the earth, she told her he had done well though he went, yet the girl would not be convinced, unable to think he could come back unharmed through the waste where bowmen with red-shafted arrows take travellers' lives and even the starving jackal turns back from the rotting dead; now he has come back with his wealth.
164.nuance: The jackal that will not go near the dead (குறுகல் செல்லாது) measures the road: too dreadful even for the scavenger, so the girl's disbelief was fair, and the friend's news answers fear rather than reproach.

colophon.thurai: பொருள் முடித்து வந்தான் என்பது வாயில்கள்வாய்க் கேட்ட தோழி தலைவிக்கு உரைத்தது

thinai_evidence.note: sun-cracked earth and a waste of robbers

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the news came through the messengers (வாயில்கள்)

165.reading: The friend tells the girl that the hill man, from a land where a hunter whose arrow missed a fierce-eyed wild cow decides the mountain held a god and goes up with his kin to worship the peak, keeps telling her how hard it is to meet, yet never says the word that would end it, while marriage messages from other suitors keep multiplying.
165.nuance: The hunter puts his failed shot down to the hill's divinity and goes to worship rather than shoot again; set beside a lover who only complains of difficulty, it may hint at a man who blames obstacles instead of acting, but only one point maps, so it stays scene. Lines 7 and 8 are hard to construe.

colophon.thurai: நொதுமலர் வரையும் பருவத்து தோழி தலைவிக்கு அறத்தொடு நிலை பயப்பச் சொல்லியது வரைவு மலிந்ததூஉம் ஆம்

thinai_evidence.note: the hill hunter and the hill man

166.reading: To his wife, changed by signs that he means to leave, the man says her body and fragrant dark hair are like gold and sapphire, her eyes and shoulders like flowers and bamboo; whenever he sees them his heart fills and he is like those settled in virtue; their son with gold bracelets has learnt to play, and he has no work in another land, so why should he part from her, when his love is greater than the sea?
166.nuance: He answers her fear with an inventory of the home: her beauty, his settled virtue, the son's first games, no work abroad. Saying that delight at home makes him like those established in aram (அறம் நிலைபெற்றோர் அனையேன்) treats the household as the seat of virtue, and the very fullness of the denial is the kind of excess a wife reads as a sign.

colophon.thurai: செலவுக் குறிப்பினால் வேறுபட்ட கிழத்திக்குத் தலைவன் சொல்லியது

thinai_evidence.note: a feared parting, which he denies

comparisons.tenor: her body and her dark hair

167.reading: The friend tells the bard who came with the shore lord's message, a knower of profitable songs and free of care, that his humble words will not remove the pallor spread over the crescent-bright forehead of the bangled girl, who lost her beauty in the fragrant grove where punnai and fresh ngaazhal flowers fall; on that shore the white heron, a guest on the punnai's westward-bending branch, cries with the sound of the tuned chariots bards received at Aay's generous feast-day assembly.
167.nuance: Each compliment to the bard is barbed: he knows songs that bring gain, he is free of grief, and his master's shore rings with the chariots bards win from Aay. This bard's errand earns nothing here; the only thing spread on his master's shore is the pallor (பாஅய பசப்பே) the master left.

colophon.thurai: தோழி பாணற்கு வாயில் மறுத்தது தூதொடு வந்த பாணற்குச் சொல்லியதூஉம் ஆம்

thinai_evidence.note: the shore grove of punnai and ngaazhal

168.reading: The friend asks the lord of the good hill, where honey that birds have pierced from a comb on the vengai branch drips into a rock hollow and the young of the dull-headed female monkey lick what the hill children left, whether it can be called good conduct to come at midnight, in the thick dark of the dread snake, down the narrow black path with only his spear for company, his chest fragrant with sandal, to their small village on the slope, not thinking of the dear life of the girl who lives loving him.
168.nuance: The scene descends in shares: bees open the flowers, birds pierce the comb, the hill children drink, the monkey's young lick the leftovers. A reader may sense a love enjoyed by stealth and in pieces, but nothing in the poem anchors a second correspondence, so it stays scene. The reproach is for her life (இன் உயிர்), not his: his danger is her danger.

colophon.thurai: தோழி இரவுக்குறி மறுத்தது

thinai_evidence.note: the midnight tryst on the hill slope

169.reading: On his way back with the task done, the man tells his heart: if we have finished what we set out to do, will you chirp, lizard of the long wall, to end the worry of the fair-browed one who waits saying he will come, in our great house in the small village, where at evening the strong-handed herdsman, turning back the leading sheep, plucks the jasmine that has climbed over the kalli on the gravel and weaves it with white palm strips into a garland whose scent fills the street?
169.nuance: He does not wait for her omen: he speaks to the lizard as if he could make it chirp, so the sign she listens for at home becomes a message he would send. The herdsman's jasmine garland scenting the street at dusk is the mullai evening at its gentlest, the hour she is likeliest to grieve.

colophon.thurai: வினை முற்றி மறுத்தராநின்றான் நெஞ்சிற்கு உரைத்தது

thinai_evidence.note: jasmine, a herdsman and sheep at dusk

170.reading: Turning away the dancer sent for the husband, the friend describes a girl with innocent eyes, tagaram-scented hair, bamboo-smooth arms, white teeth and close thighs, wearing a leaf skirt, who has come alone and stands making the festival ground shine; rise, rise, she cries, to guard our husband, and yet, as the many Aryans thronging famous Mullur fled before the single spear of Malaiyan of the bright sword, what use are our numbers if this one woman's strength prevails?
170.nuance: The wives speak as an army and the rival as a lone champion, and the borrowed battle runs against them: in the story the many fled and the one won. The friend turns the household's numbers into a joke at its own expense, and the joke is her refusal: the dancer's errand is pointless when the husband is already won. The colophon gives the speech to the friend, though எம் கொழுநன் sounds like the wives' own voice.

colophon.thurai: தோழி விறலிக்கு வாயில் மறுத்தது

thinai_evidence.note: wives guarding a husband against a festival dancer

comparisons.tenor: the many wives helpless before one rival

171.reading: Told that the man will leave, the friend says to the girl: he comes from a land where the elephant, straining for water on the scorched summer slope, leaves behind its soft-headed calf that cannot keep pace, and the calf, to the pity of the village women, walks into the town with the cows' calves; if he crosses the many-hilled hard waste and leaves us, how will her eyes bear it, eyes used to lying on his chest with eager heart at midnight, the hour the ghosts walk?
171.nuance: The calf left behind by a herd gone for water is a near miss for iraicchi: one carrier, and its plight is hers, but it does nothing a person of the situation does; it is the one abandoned, and the poem never draws the parallel. A land where even a strayed calf is taken in sharpens the question of who will take her in. Lines 7 to 9 (ஞாங்க ... நிகர்ப்ப) are obscure.

colophon.thurai: பிரிவு உணர்த்தப்பட்ட தோழி தலைமகட்கு உரைத்தது

thinai_evidence.note: the man is to cross the waste and leave her

172.reading: The friend tells the shore lord who has come for a daytime meeting that as girls at play they pressed a seed into the white sand and forgot it; when it sprouted they raised it with sweet milk and ghee, and their mother said this punnai is your elder sister, nobler than you; so they are ashamed to laugh with him beneath it, and if he means to grant them grace there are other shades, on his shore where the white right-spiralled conch sounds like the pale music of guest bards.
172.nuance: The mother's word makes the tree kin, and kin may not witness a secret meeting: the friend's shame is a polite fiction that turns the tryst away and points him to the one proper shade, marriage, which நீ நல்கின் says without saying it.

colophon.thurai: பகற்குறி வந்த தலைமகனைத் தோழி வரைவு கடாயது குறிபெயர்த்தீடும் ஆம்

thinai_evidence.note: the punnai on the white sand and the conch of the shore

comparisons.tenor: the sound of the right-spiralled conch

173.reading: With the man listening outside, the friend asks the girl: the mother who loves them took for the god's seizure what followed his gifts of spring flowers, garlands and red kaanthal chaplets of the hill, and has it shown in waking and in dreams; if she is told that the lord of that gem-bright mountain caused this sickness, which comes no other way, would that wrong tall Vel of the bee-loud green garland? Tell me, bangled one, I ask.
173.nuance: The question is a move, not a scruple: asking whether naming the man would offend Murugan lets the overhearing lover know that disclosure (அறத்தொடு நிலை) is near and that the veri rite is being held for the wrong cause.

colophon.thurai: தோழி தலைவிக்கு உரைப்பாளாய் சிறைப்புறமாகச் சொல்லியது வெறி அச்சுறீஇத் தோழி அறத்தொடு நிலை பயப்பித்ததூஉம் ஆம்

thinai_evidence.note: hill-spring flowers, red kaanthal and Murugan

occasion.words: வெறி அச்சுறீஇத் தோழி அறத்தொடு நிலை பயப்பித்ததூஉம்

174.reading: To the friend who says that though her lover is back from the windy waste, where the lone palmyra bears fruit like ripe date clusters and the tiger walks when the male call sounds from its branch, and has embraced her sweetly and stays by her without parting, she is still wasted, the girl answers that it may look so to those who do not know: he has given his rich chest to a woman who takes without loving, and what is an embrace worth where there is no love?
174.nuance: The friend measures the return by presence (பிரியாது ஒரு வழி உறையினும); the girl measures it by love and finds it gone. The paalai waste of the opening is only the road he came back by; the grief is a marutham grief, another woman at his chest. வீழாக் கொள்கை வீழ்ந்த கொண்டி is compressed and its sense is not certain.

colophon.thurai: வினை முற்றி வந்து எய்திய காலத்து ஆற்றாளாய தலைவியைத் தோழி வற்புறீஇ நின்றாட்கு அவள் சொல்லியது

thinai_evidence.note: a returned husband who has another woman

175.reading: With the man listening, the friend says that the mother does not even know the lord of the shore, where fishermen who tossed on the long sea in curved boats heap their fat catch on the sand and sleep by small lamps of shells filled with fish oil under the fragrant punnai; yet at midnight, trusting the petty talk of the hamlet women, she looks as if to burn at my body, pale as boiled milk.
175.nuance: The mother has never seen the man and judges by gossip alone, so her burning look falls on the only evidence she can see, the pallor. The fishermen's small shell lamps, fires that let them sleep, stand against a mother's look that lets the girl have no rest.

colophon.thurai: தோழி சிறைப்புறமாகச் சொல்லியது

thinai_evidence.note: fishermen, shell lamps and punnai on the shore

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the pallor is spoken of in the first person (என் பசலை); the friend speaks in the girl's voice or the girl speaks

176.reading: The other woman, speaking to a dancer so that those close to the wife's friend may hear, asks whether the wife can really claim to love the man when she does not know how to keep him with grace, since she herself loved him and freely let him go; and she points to their home, a hill-fenced village on the plantain slope where red kaanthal bursts from the bud like the stripes on elephants' faces and bees hum like a lute to the drum of the falling stream.
176.nuance: The boast carries a jab: the rival says she let him go out of generosity, so his being at home is her gift, not the wife's hold. The soft hill-slope ending, bees and waterfall in one music, makes the wife's home sound idyllic only to say it could not keep him. Lines 1 to 4 are compressed and the sense is not fixed.

colophon.thurai: பரத்தை தலைவியின் பாங்கிக்குப் பாங்காயினார் கேட்ப விறலிக்குச் சொல்லியது

thinai_evidence.note: a rival's taunt about the wife is marutham matter though the setting is the hill

comparisons.tenor: the red kaanthal bursting from the bud
the sound of the falling stream

thurai_akam.speaker: parathai
thurai_akam.note: the overhearers are those close to the wife's friend

177.reading: Reading his signs, the girl tells her friend that he has already crossed in mind the hot, hard waste where spreading fire wears down the forest and the trees burn; she has seen it in his ways: his spear is wiped bright along the blade, his shield crowned with peacock feathers and hung with bells, and he is far more tender than before; now, friend, the day seems to have come when the pupils of her painted eyes, aching again and again, will swim in a rising flood.
177.nuance: She reads two signs together, the war gear made ready and the excess of tenderness (பண்டினும் நனி பல அளிப்ப); either alone would mean little. Her tears become a flood the little figure in her eye must swim, grief turned into a drowning.

colophon.thurai: செலவுக் குறிப்பு அறிந்த தலைமகள் தோழிக்கு உரைத்தது

thinai_evidence.note: she reads a coming parting from his signs

178.reading: With the man standing by, the friend says that the chariot of the lord of the cool shore, where the poor female heron, whose beauty her big-legged mate with crest feathers like finely kneaded soft pith has enjoyed, will not eat the small fish at the backwater's edge but sits in loneliness on the drooping kaithai branch, could once be seen with the eyes; now, ashamed, I get no sleep even in the dead of night, I take every bird cry for his bells and listen, and my heart that trusted him has perished.
178.nuance: The heron hen carries the whole situation unspoken: enjoyed and left (நலன் உணப்பட்ட), she will not eat, and she sits alone, as the girl, now kept at home (செறிப்பு), wastes and cannot sleep. The friend speaks the last lines in the girl's first person.

colophon.thurai: சிறைப்புறமாகத் தோழி செறிப்பு அறிவுறீஇயது

thinai_evidence.note: the heron on the kaithai by the backwater

comparisons.tenor: the cries of birds in the night
the girl, enjoyed and then left alone

ullurai.tenor: the girl and the shore lord who enjoyed her love and now stays away

pairs.situation: her beauty was taken in the secret union
she is now kept apart at home and lives alone

ullurai.speaker_fit: the friend uses a heron of the neythal backwater in a neythal poem (porul 7.27)

179.reading: The foster mother recalls that when the calving cow ate the vayalai creeper growing by the house, her girl threw her ball to the ground, cast away her doll and beat her own belly, and with a bewildered look like a doe's would not drink the honey and sweet milk she and the mother pressed on her but swelled with sobs; she was like that only yesterday, and today they say she has crossed the hard waste trusting the false word of a dark-bearded youth, opening her budding smile of white teeth like peacock-quill tips.
179.nuance: The poem ends on a smile: the child who sobbed over a creeper and refused milk from two mothers goes off smiling, and the bewilderment at home (மனை மருட்சி) is at that change. The speaker's யானும் தாயும் makes her the foster mother.

colophon.thurai: மனை மருட்சி

thinai_evidence.note: the girl has gone across the waste with a youth

thurai_akam.speaker: sevili
thurai_akam.note: the colophon names only the theme; the speaker is the foster mother, at home, to no one named

180.reading: The friend, who had let the husband in, seeing the wife's jealousy says: the man of the town where the field heron rubs against the ant-swarmed nest on the bitter gourd and the ants spill like white rice mixed with red paddy, wanting many women, does not come to our house, and she, trusting her dark beauty, will not let him go; like the ruin of the punnai felled on the battlefield of two great kings, Anni great and the other greater, this quarrel of the two of them will end with me.
180.nuance: The friend casts herself as the punnai, the tree destroyed because two powers fought over it, and the go-between who let the husband in fears she will pay for the couple's quarrel. The heron breaking the ants' nest is a near miss for ullurai (a man breaking a household), but only one pair maps. Who trusts the dark beauty in line 5 is not certain.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகற்கு வாயில் நேர்ந்த தோழி தலைமகளிடத்துப் பொறாமை கண்டு சொல்லியது

thinai_evidence.note: the field pond, paddy and the heron

comparisons.tenor: the ants spilling from the broken nest
the friend's ruin between the quarrelling pair

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon names no addressee; she speaks of the wife and husband as 'these two'

links.note: Both returning men, speaking to the charioteer, picture the wife with the same words, the freckle-waisted woman who deceives their son (புதல்வற் பொய்க்கும், திதலை அல்குல்); Akananuru 54 fills it with her promising the moon milk for a gold tali, Natrinai 161 with her pointing out strangers to the boy.
links.teaches: The shared phrase shows that soothing the son with a fiction was a fixed mullai picture of the home a returning man imagines, and the two fillings show where the poet's freedom lay: in choosing the fiction, a coaxed moon or a stranger passed off as the father.

links.note: Both men are going home with the task done; in 161 he wonders whether the omen birds have already told her, in 169 he speaks to the house lizard and asks it to chirp for her.
links.teaches: Together they show the returning husband imagining the omen from her side and then trying to work it from his own, so the signs she watches for become signs he wishes he could send.

links.note: Kural 49 says that what is called virtue is household life; in Natrinai 166 a husband says that seeing his wife he is like those settled in virtue, and gives that and his son's first play as reasons he will not leave.
links.teaches: The poem shows the Kural's claim used as an argument against the paalai journey: a husband offers the household's settled virtue as his answer to the pull of wealth abroad, which makes the maxim a reason to stay.

links.note: In Akananuru 66 the sight of his small son stops a husband on his way to a second wedding; in Natrinai 166 the husband himself names his son's first games as one reason he will not leave.
links.teaches: Read together, the son is the akam poets' anchor of the husband to the house, named by the man himself in 166 and working against his intent in 66, so in both the wife's fear is answered by the child rather than by her own claim on him.

links.note: Purananuru 127 praises Aay, whose bards led away his elephants and whose palace stood bare from giving; Natrinai 167 makes the rattle of the chariots bards won at Aay's feast the sound of a heron's cry on the shore of the man whose bard the friend turns away.
links.teaches: The pairing shows an akam friend borrowing Aay's puram fame as the measure of a generous patron, so the bard who in puram goes home rich is in akam the go-between sent home empty: one profession seen from the giver's hall and from the wronged wife's door.

links.note: In Akananuru 72 the girl says the man who came through the midnight rain with only a spear for company (எஃகு துணையாக) is not cruel and the fault is hers; in Natrinai 168 the friend asks the man who comes at midnight with his spear for company (எஃகு துணை ஆக) whether that can be called good conduct. The same act is blameless in one and a failure of conduct in the other.
links.teaches: The same lone midnight journey is innocent to the girl and faulty to the friend, which shows the night tryst was judged by who spoke: the girl takes the blame on herself, while the friend's charge is her lever toward marriage.

links.note: In Akananuru 351 the returning man pictures the lizard chirping at her ear as she worships the omen birds; in Natrinai 169 he speaks to the lizard on the long wall and asks whether it will chirp to end her worry.
links.teaches: Together they show the house lizard as an oracle both ends of the separation rely on: she listens for it at home, and he, on the road, begs it to speak for him.

links.note: Purananuru 123 praises Malaiyan for chariots given more freely than the raindrops on the peak of Mullur; Natrinai 170 recalls Malaiyan's single spear routing the many Aryans at Mullur, as the image of wives helpless before one rival.
links.teaches: Held together they show a chieftain's fame had two faces, giving and lone valour, and the akam poet chose the war face because the household's problem was one woman beating many: akam borrowed from puram exactly the facet its situation needed.

links.note: In Akananuru 388 the girl would ask the mother's velan whether his god goes hunting on a deer's track with a bloody arrow; in Natrinai 173 the friend asks whether saying that the hill lord caused the sickness would wrong Murugan.
links.teaches: Both turn the veri rite's diagnosis against itself by slipping the real cause, the hill man, into a question about the god, which shows that disclosure (அறத்தொடு நிலை) had a recognised form: a mock-pious question put within the lover's hearing.

links.note: Kural 1311 has the woman refuse her man's chest because all women feast on him with their eyes; in Natrinai 174 the wife, told she should be well now that he is back and never leaves her side, says he gave his chest to another woman and an embrace is worth nothing without love.
links.teaches: The Kural grounds the refusal in shared possession; the poem grounds it in absent love even when he is wholly present, so the pair separates two grievances the oodal chapters run together: that he is shared, and that he is there without love.

links.note: Kural 1147 says love's sickness grows with the town's gossip as manure and the mother's words as water; Natrinai 175 shows a mother who has never met the man, believing the hamlet women's petty talk, glaring at the girl's pale body at midnight.
links.teaches: The poem supplies the order the couplet only implies: the gossip reaches the mother first and her watch follows from it, so she acts on hearsay about a man she does not know, which is why her words feed the sickness instead of curing it.

links.note: Kural 1276: the woman tells her friend that his great comfort and eager lovemaking hold the hardship to come and the thought of his lack of love; in Natrinai 177 the girl tells her friend she reads his going in his being more tender than before, along with his spear wiped and his shield decked.
links.teaches: The couplet names one sign, excess tenderness; the poem shows it read together with the readied weapons, so the Kural's inference is the abstract of a scene in which caress and war gear together give the man away.

links.note: In Akananuru 17 the foster mother remembers her girl tiring at a little ball play and lying in her arms, and asks whether those feet can walk the waste; in Natrinai 179 the nurse recalls the girl sobbing and refusing milk over a creeper the cow ate, and hears she has crossed the waste smiling.
links.teaches: Both measure the elopement by remembered childish frailty, but 179 ends on the girl's smile, so the pair shows the nurse's lament with two endings: fear for a frail child in 17, and in 179 bewilderment that a child who wept at a small loss left without grief.

links.note: Both use the punnai felled in the war of Anni and Thithiyan as a simile: in Akananuru 145 the foster mother wishes on her own hand the ruin of that tree; in Natrinai 180 the friend fears she will be ruined like it in the quarrel of husband and wife.
links.teaches: Read together, the felled guardian tree was a stock figure of ruin, and 180 draws from it what 145 does not need, the tree's innocence: it is the bystander destroyed because two powers fought over it, which is the go-between's place in a marriage quarrel.
